vignette:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

A permanent pacemaker was placed on day 50, with transient clinical improvement. Two days later, he again developed fever and elevated C-reactive protein but had negative cultures and completed another week of antibiotics. He was weaned to high-flow nasal cannula by day 64 but required reintubation within 24 hours of weaning. A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. vignette:
A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the right upper posterior tooth region that had grown progressively, causing facial asymmetry. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Examination revealed a 4.0×3.5 cm diffuse, well-defined, hard, nontender swelling on the right middle third of the face, extending from 1 cm below the infraorbital margin to the inferior border of the mandible and from the ala of the nose posteriorly to the anterior border of the ramus. The overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, there was a 4.0×3.0 cm ovoid, hard, nontender swelling in the right buccal vestibule with buccal cortical expansion and slight palatal expansion but no mucosal changes. A provisional clinical diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma was made, with fibrous dysplasia as a consideration. 

Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a ground-glass trabecular pattern with radiolucency around the roots of deciduous teeth and erupting premolars. A maxillary occlusal film demonstrated increased radiopacity, buccal cortical expansion, and a ground-glass appearance without palatal involvement. Cone-beam CT revealed expansion of the buccal and palatal cortical plates, involvement of more than half of the right maxillary sinus, a well-defined margin, and a ground-glass internal pattern. Based on these images, a radiological diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma of the right posterior maxilla was made, with fibrous dysplasia considered less likely because “the margin of the swelling was well-defined and well demarcated from the surrounding areas which was very much unlike FD whose margin is ill-defined and merges with the surrounding areas.”

By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of epilepsy presented with redness and swelling of the right breast. On examination, there was erythema and swelling in the lower right breast. Ultrasound revealed a 54 × 41 × 31 mm low-echo mass with partially unclear margins in the outer right breast. Biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), high grade, ER+, PgR–, HER2 3+, Ki67 70%. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased uptake in the right axilla, anterior mediastinum, left pleura, and liver, consistent with cT4dN3M1 stage IV breast cancer. She received four cycles of FEC chemotherapy, after which lesions nearly disappeared, and then trastuzumab plus pertuzumab with docetaxel, achieving a clinical complete response maintained for 23 months. Two years after treatment initiation, she developed a persistent headache. CT and MRI of the head revealed a 30-mm mass lesion in the right temporal lobe.
